---
# Where Flatness Comes From

Suppose you want to make a flat surface, one flat enough that a machinist would trust it as a reference for checking other work. The obvious method is to compare your piece against something already known to be flat and remove metal wherever the two disagree. That method works, and nearly every flat thing in the world is made that way. It also raises a question about the reference, and about whatever the reference was checked against, and so on down the chain. At some point somebody made a flat surface with nothing flat to copy.

How they did it is my favourite problem in the history of technology. We live surrounded by precision we rarely notice. A piston fits its cylinder with a clearance of a few hundredths of a millimetre. The balls in a decent bicycle bearing are round to within about a micrometre. All of this descends from machine tools, which were built with earlier machine tools. Follow the family tree back and it narrows to a few workshops in England around 1800, where people worked with files, chisels, and hand-forged iron. The strange part is that each generation of machines came out more accurate than the generation that built it. Copies are normally worse than originals. In this lineage the copies kept improving for two centuries, and the reasons are specific enough to explain.

Start with flatness. Take three cast iron plates, each roughly flat, and call them A, B, and C. Smear A with a thin film of pigment (Prussian blue in oil is traditional) and rub it against B. The blue transfers to B wherever B stands high. Take a hand scraper, which is a hardened blade on a long handle, and shave those blue spots down, a few thousandths of a millimetre per stroke. Rub again, scrape again. After many rounds, A and B touch each other all over.

This proves less than it seems to. A might be a shallow dome and B a matching bowl, and the two would fit perfectly while both being wrong. So you bring in C and fit it to A in the same way. If A is a dome, then B and C are now both bowls, and when you rub B against C they touch only around their rims. The blue shows the disagreement at once. You scrape B and C toward each other, return to A, and keep cycling through the pairs, turning the plates a quarter turn now and then so that a saddle-shaped twist can't hide. A dome fits a bowl, but a bowl doesn't fit another bowl. The only surface that mates with a copy of itself is a plane, so three plates that all fit each other in every pairing must be flat.

Joseph Whitworth described the method in a paper in 1840. He had trained in Henry Maudslay's London workshop, where something like it was probably already in use, and his own contribution was to insist on scraping instead of grinding the plates together with abrasive paste. Whoever deserves the credit, what I admire is that the process takes in no accuracy from outside. The rough plates are inaccurate, the scraper is a hand tool, and the worker's eye can't see the errors being corrected. The flatness comes from the geometry of the situation, from a property that planes have and no other surface does, turned into a shop routine that a patient person can follow.

Once you have seen this pattern you find it throughout precision engineering. The simplest version is the reversal. Set a spirit level on a table and note where the bubble sits. Turn the level end for end and set it in the same spot. If the bubble sits in the same place relative to the vial, the level is true. If it moves, the level is off by half the difference, and the table's tilt is the average of the two readings. You have measured the table and the instrument at once, with no second level to check the first.

A carpenter tests a square the same way. He draws a line along its blade from the edge of a board, flips the square over, and draws again. The two lines diverge by twice the square's error. A straightedge is tested by ruling a line, flipping it across that line, and ruling a second one. In each case, flipping the tool reverses its error while the thing being measured stays put. The flaw ends up displayed at double size, which is convenient, because small flaws are hard to see.

Screws needed a different principle. A lathe cuts a thread by moving its cutting tool along the work at a rate set by its own lead screw, so every error in the lead screw is copied into the product. Since the first lead screws were made by hand, by filing along a line scribed around a rod, this looks like a trap. Maudslay spent years getting out of it, and one of the ways out is averaging. A nut that engages a single thread follows every wobble in that thread. A long nut that engages thirty threads at once can't follow all thirty wobbles, since they disagree with each other, so it rides on something close to their mean. Drive the cutting tool from the long nut and the screw you cut is better than the screw you started with. Put the new screw in the lathe and go around again.

By about 1805 Maudslay had a bench micrometer built around a screw good enough to resolve a ten-thousandth of an inch. The workshop called it the Lord Chancellor, because it settled disputes.

Dividing a circle into equal parts, which is what you need for gears, sextants, and anything else that measures angle, relies on a third idea. The angles around a point add up to exactly one full turn. Nobody has to measure this; it follows from what a circle is. So if you step around a divided circle comparing each interval with its neighbour, the discrepancies have to sum to zero, and whatever fails to cancel is your own error, ready to be divided up and corrected. Instrument makers call this closure. Jesse Ramsden built a dividing engine on these lines in the 1770s, and the sextants it produced went to sea and found longitude with them.

So flatness, squareness, straightness, uniform screws, and equal angles can all be generated from nothing, because each is a matter of shape, and shape can be checked against itself. Length is different. Geometry tells you whether two things are the same size, but it has no opinion about how big an inch should be. For that you need an agreed object, and for most of history the agreed objects were bad. Every workshop had its own rule and its own gauges, and a bolt made in one factory would not fit a nut made in the next.

The person who did the most to fix this was a Swede named Carl Edvard Johansson, an inspector at the state rifle factory in Eskilstuna. In 1896 he visited the Mauser works in Germany, where every dimension of every rifle part had its own dedicated gauge, thousands of them, each a separate thing to make and maintain. The story goes that he worked out an alternative on the train home. Instead of one gauge per dimension, make a small set of steel blocks whose sizes are chosen like the weights in a weighing set, so that stacking a few of them gives any length you want. His first set had about a hundred blocks and could be combined to produce some twenty thousand different lengths in steps of a hundredth of a millimetre.

For this to work, the blocks had to be far more accurate than the steps between them, since the errors add when you stack. The faces also had to be so flat and smooth that no gap was left between one block and the next. Johansson reportedly did his early finishing work at home, on a lapping machine converted from his wife's sewing machine. The blocks he produced had a property that still startles people who handle them for the first time. Slide two together with a slight twist and they stick, firmly enough that a stack can be picked up by its top block. Machinists call this wringing. The usual explanation involves an extremely thin film of oil or moisture plus attraction between the surfaces themselves, and the effect is reported to persist in a vacuum, so air pressure isn't the main cause.

Gauge blocks gave factories a way to carry the same length from one building to another. Henry Leland, who ran Cadillac, is usually credited with bringing the first set to America, and in 1908 Cadillac won the Dewar Trophy in England with a stunt that depended on that kind of discipline. Three cars were taken apart, their parts were shuffled into one heap, and three cars were rebuilt from the heap and driven around the Brooklands track. Henry Ford later went further and hired Johansson himself, who moved to Dearborn in 1923.

Johansson also settled the inch, more or less by himself. The British and American inches differed by a few parts per million, which mattered at the accuracy he was working to. He made his inch blocks to exactly 25.4 millimetres, a value that fell between the two. Industry adopted his blocks, so industry adopted his inch, and in 1959 the governments concerned made it official.

Working at this level brings up a complication that I enjoy very much, which is temperature. Steel expands by about eleven or twelve parts per million for each degree Celsius. A hundred-millimetre gauge block held in a warm hand for a minute grows by a micrometre or more, which is larger than the tolerance it was made to. So a length, stated carefully, always comes with a temperature attached. The agreed figure since 1931 has been twenty degrees. Metrology labs hold their rooms there, handle blocks with gloves or tongs, and leave a part sitting on the surface plate for hours before measuring it so that it can settle to the temperature of the room. The practice is called soaking. A steel bar is always slowly changing size, and measuring it means catching it at an agreed moment.

The story ends with length joining the other quantities. In 1960 the metre stopped being the distance between two scratches on a platinum-iridium bar in a vault outside Paris and became a certain number of wavelengths of light from krypton. In 1983 it was redefined again as the distance light travels in a vacuum in 1/299,792,458 of a second. Gauge blocks are now calibrated by interferometry, which amounts to counting light waves along their length. The standard of size, the one thing that had always depended on a particular object kept in a particular place, can now be regenerated by anyone with the right equipment. The kilogram followed in 2019.

I should admit that I have never scraped a plate or wrung two blocks together. I know all of this from what people have written, above all Wayne Moore's *Foundations of Mechanical Accuracy*, a 1970 book from a Connecticut toolmaking firm that treats the subject with a seriousness close to devotion. What draws me to it is the structure of the reasoning more than the hardware. In each case nobody has access to the true answer, and nobody needs it. They arrange for errors to oppose one another, by using a third plate, a reversal, a long nut, or a closed circle, and they keep what is left after the cancellation.

I think about this in connection with my own position, since most of what I know comes from comparing accounts with each other, with no master reference to consult. The analogy is useful mainly for where it breaks. Two plates that fit each other perfectly can both be wrong, the dome and the bowl, and two sources that agree can be wrong in the same complementary way, each shaped by the other. The third plate works only because geometry guarantees that a shared error cannot survive all three pairings. Nothing guarantees that for testimony. Three accounts can agree and all be mistaken if they share an origin. So the lesson I take from Whitworth is narrower than "check things against each other." Agreement counts as evidence only when the comparison is set up so that a common error would have to show itself. Designing that kind of comparison is most of the work, in a machine shop and outside one.

The best machine tools are still finished this way. The sliding surfaces of a high-grade grinding machine are scraped by hand, by someone reading blue marks and shaving off high spots, because no machine yet cuts a surface as true as one made by that slow process of comparison. The result isn't smooth. Under raking light it shows a field of small plateaus, twenty or thirty to the square inch, with shallow hollows between them that hold oil.

If you own a spirit level, you can run the oldest of these checks yourself in about a minute. Set it down, read it, turn it end for end, and read it again. If the bubble moves, you have learned something about your level that no label on it could have told you.
---

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW. This is a technically detailed essay with a distinctive voice, personal enthusiasms, and an explicit turn from engineering into a reflection on knowledge.

## Grounded reading
The voice is patient and quietly delighted by ingenious ways to make accuracy without an unquestionable reference. Its pathos lies less in machinery itself than in the ingenuity of people who can make errors reveal one another: three plates, a reversed level, a long nut, a closed circle. The first-person passages make the technical tour feel personally chosen, especially the admission that the author has never done the work but is drawn to its reasoning. The essay invites readers to try a simple check themselves, while also asking them to be more careful about what agreement between sources can establish.

## What the model chose to foreground
The sample foregrounds self-correcting systems, standards, precision craft, and the limits of inference. It repeatedly returns to comparison and cancellation as ways to expose error, then distinguishes mechanical checks from testimony, where shared origins can leave shared mistakes intact. It also gives attention to tangible details—the blue pigment, the “Lord Chancellor,” wringing gauge blocks, temperature-sensitive steel, and scraped surfaces under raking light—alongside a mood of admiration for patient, exacting work.

## Evidence line
> The flatness comes from the geometry of the situation, from a property that planes have and no other surface does, turned into a shop routine that a patient person can follow.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
High, because the essay sustains a distinctive combination of technical explanation, material detail, personal fascination, and careful epistemic reflection from beginning to end.
